Biomolecular emulators · solution scattering · experimental design

Where does BioEmu-1 fail against solution scattering, and what should be measured next?

Natalija Stepurko · October 2026 · natalija-stepurko.com

BioEmu-1 [1] predicts the set of shapes a protein adopts in solution from its sequence. I asked where these predicted ensembles disagree with measurements, and which new measurements would test and improve such a model. As a benchmark, I compared raw BioEmu-1 ensembles with small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) profiles from SASBDB [4], using the ensembles and computed curves that the PeptoneBench authors published [3]. The clearest systematic error ran opposite to my expectation: for disordered proteins the ensembles are too extended. The obstacle for choosing new experiments is prediction: the size of the error on a protein could not be predicted before measuring it. The proposed campaign therefore has two arms, a controlled replication of known discrepancies and a prospective test of the extension bias.

All the code is public. Every number and figure on this page comes from the pipeline in this repository, which downloads the public inputs, scores them and writes the campaign proposal.Natalija-Stepurko/bioemu-saxs-campaign

How the benchmark works

SAXS reports the overall size and shape of a protein in solution, averaged over every conformation it adopts, so it tests an ensemble as a whole. BioEmu-1 was trained on predicted structures, molecular-dynamics simulations and measured stabilities [1]. BioEmu conformers have served as a pool for SAXS ensemble selection on a few dozen proteins, where the unweighted pool did not reproduce the data [2], and PeptoneBench ranks generators by their fit after reweighting [3]. This study asks where the raw model fails by protein class and what that implies for the next measurements.

This project re-analyses BioEmu-1 ensembles sampled by the PeptoneBench authors; it does not retrain or re-sample the model. The archive records the BioEmu code version but not the checkpoint.

The eight steps of the pipeline
  1. public input
    439 measured SAXS profiles with sequence, pH and per-residue disorder score: PeptoneDB-SAXS, curated from SASBDB [4, 3].
  2. public input
    100 BioEmu-1 conformers per protein, sampled by the PeptoneBench authors from the sequence alone.
  3. public input
    One scattering curve per conformer, computed by the PeptoneBench authors with Pepsi-SAXS [6] on each profile's q grid.
  4. computed here
    Average the conformer curves with equal weights; fit one scale factor [5] and one constant background; report reduced χ² against the measured errors, and NRMSD, a second score that does not weight by them.
  5. computed here
    Guinier radius of gyration of the data and of the ensemble curve; flags for aggregation (low-angle upturn), over-subtraction (intensity below −3σ) and oligomers (SASBDB measured mass against sequence mass).
  6. computed here
    Maximum-entropy reweighting [7] along a path of decreasing prior strength; the effective sample fraction φ at the first point with χ² ≤ 2 sorts each entry into one of four kinds.
  7. computed here
    The same scoring for 6 comparator models on the shared entries: four ensemble generators and two single-structure predictors as reference baselines.
  8. computed here
    Predict the raw error from features known before measuring; compare acquisition policies on held-out folds; select replication systems by stated rules and write the two-arm campaign.

Raw SAXS fit is worse for disordered proteins, but the size of the gap depends on how error is measured

Each raw ensemble is the uniform average of its conformer curves, scaled to the profile with one factor and one constant background. Of the 399 profiles, 146 meet χ² ≤ 2 (37%, 95% interval 32%–41%). The median raw χ² is 8.9 for disordered and 2.3 for folded proteins (4.3 for partly disordered). Under NRMSD, a deviation of ln I that does not weight points by their reported errors, the class medians are similar: 0.030 folded, 0.034 partly disordered and 0.031 disordered, with overlapping intervals. A poor reduced χ² can reflect both the disagreement with the curve and the precision assigned to the measurement. The size error is examined separately below.

What a fit looks like

One protein per class, the one nearest its class median of raw χ², shows the fits on measured curves.

How to read Figure 2

Residuals. (Imodel − Iexp)/σ against q, with ±3 guides. A residual that wanders outside ±3 over a range of q is a shape error at that length scale (about 1/q); a flat band within ±3 is a fit at the noise level.

Reweighted curve. The reweighted curve is taken where the four kinds are read, at the first point along the reweighting path with χ² ≤ 2 (φ 0.96 for SASDH84, φ 0.90 for SASDM65, φ 0.84 for SASDLK9). φ is the effective sample fraction the weights keep, 1 for uniform weights. The χ² minimum of each path is 1.15 at φ 0.021, 0.99 at φ 0.080, 0.93 at φ 0.085 (folded, partly disordered, disordered); a minimum at small φ rests on a few conformers and overfits.

Envelope. DENSS [8] reconstructions from the measured curve alone (ten maps, aligned and averaged; Dmax from the SASBDB record), drawn as filled projections of two density levels of the averaged map: the isosurface enclosing the protein's expected volume at 1.7 Å³ per Da (darker) and the one enclosing the volume DENSS assigned to the particle (lighter). The conformer is the highest-weight one at the χ² minimum of the path, docked into the protein-volume level by principal axes; the share of its Cα atoms inside that level is given under each panel and, for both levels, in the table. The drawn conformer has breaks in the sampled chain (consecutive Cα more than 4.2 Å apart): 5 in SASDM65, 24 in SASDLK9.

How typical the examples are. Each is the entry nearest its class median of raw χ². SASDLK9 is not typical in size: its size ratio (1.09) is below the disordered median (1.21), so this column understates the class-wide excess. It is 475 residues long, and the drawn conformer has 24 chain breaks.

What the envelope is. An illustration from an ensemble-averaged measurement, not evidence about any single conformation; for a disordered protein one conformer cannot fill it.

Disordered ensembles are systematically too extended

The radius of gyration, Rg, is the root-mean-square distance of a protein's mass from its centre, a single number for overall size; SAXS measures it from the lowest-angle part of the curve. For disordered proteins the median ensemble size is 21% above experiment from the scattering curves and 35% above from the conformer coordinates.

E4 expected the usual failure of models trained on folded data, over-compaction of disordered chains. The data show the opposite: the median ratio is 1.21 (95% interval 1.12–1.28, two-sided Wilcoxon p < 0.001, n = 41), and 76% of disordered entries lie above 1; folded proteins sit at 0.98. The size discrepancy is also present in coordinate-derived radii: the Cα radius of the sampled conformers is 1.35 times the measured value (1.20–1.47). Cα, full-atom and SAXS-derived radii are different observables, however: for folded proteins the Cα ratio is 0.91 where the curve gives 0.95, an offset because the curve includes side chains and a hydration layer that the Cα radius leaves out. The 35% is therefore not to be read as an exact physical excess; it shows that the extension is present in the conformers before any curve is computed.

Can the disagreement be corrected by changing conformer populations?

Reweighting keeps every conformer fixed and adjusts only how often each one occurs, until the averaged curve matches the profile. Maximum-entropy reweighting [7] does this while keeping the weights as close to uniform as the data allow; relaxing that constraint step by step traces a path from the raw ensemble towards a full fit. The effective sample fraction φ measures how much of the ensemble still carries weight: 1 for uniform weights, near 0 when a few conformers carry it all. The four kinds are read where the path first reaches χ² ≤ 2: raw fit (already there), modestly reweightable (reached with φ ≥ 0.5), strongly reweightable (reached only with φ < 0.5, which requires substantial population changes) and target fit not reached (by the tested reweighting procedure).

Reweighting brings 183 more profiles to χ² ≤ 2, 106 of them only with φ < 0.5; for 70 the target is not reached.

Two cautions. Reweightability is not information gain: SAXS is low-dimensional, and distinct ensembles can give the same curve, so a reweighted fit does not identify the true populations. Not reaching the target does not establish that compatible conformations are absent from BioEmu's distribution; it describes this finite ensemble of 100 conformers, this forward model and this procedure.

Can the error map guide experiments on proteins that have not been measured?

An error map needs the measurement. Choosing a new experiment needs the error predicted before the measurement exists. I fitted predictors of the raw error (log₁₀ χ²) from quantities known before a profile exists: chain length, disorder score and class, sequence composition, the Rg expected from length by scaling laws [9], and the model's own ensemble Rg and conformer spread. Evaluation is 5-fold cross-validation grouped by sequence cluster, repeated five times. I then asked which entries each acquisition policy would pick from held-out folds and scored the picks by the high-discrepancy target yield: the share that are strongly reweightable or whose target fit is not reached. The yield is a proxy for where the model is wrong, not a measure of training value.

The best model explains 5% of held-out variation in the raw error (R² = 0.05; class means alone 0.04), and the tree classifier of the high-discrepancy kinds reaches an AUC of 0.59. Random picks of ten give a yield of 0.44, with a spread of ±0.15 for any single pick. Ranking by predicted error gives 0.51 ± 0.06, +0.06 over random, within about one sd of a single random pick. The acquisition policy fed predictions, the campaign's priority rule with predicted inputs, gives 0.44 ± 0.06. The oracle ranking, which uses the measured SAXS, reaches 1.00: the rule separates the kinds when it sees the measurement, and the missing piece is a predictor of them. The map therefore supports controlled replication of known failures; it does not support a new-protein campaign driven by predicted error.

The priority score is not a basis for recommending measurements. The design proposed ranking systems by log₁₀ raw χ² × a reweighting weight × a tractability weight, with weights set by judgement. Fed the quantities known before a measurement, it picks high-discrepancy profiles at 0.44 against 0.44 for random choice, a difference inside the spread of a single random pick. I report the score and its test, and the campaign below does not rest on it. Arm 1 re-measures deposited systems, so it can use their measured discrepancy directly: it lists the systems that meet stated eligibility rules and have the largest observed raw χ², which are the same twelve the score ranks first; what is dropped is the judgement-set weighting. Arm 2 splits test proteins from controls by a quantity computed from the model and the sequence alone, within the archive's disordered entries whose deposited profiles pass the quality checks.

What should be measured next?

What BioEmu-1 was trained on, what the SAXS archive covers and where the two leave gaps are the evidence for which protein data to collect. This section measures all three, relates BioEmu-1's error to closeness to its training data, and then lists the categories of proteins the evidence supports, before the two arms of the campaign.

What BioEmu-1 was trained on

BioEmu-1 learned in three stages [1]. Pre-training used 50,228 AlphaFold Database sequence clusters (179,422 predicted structures; the cluster definitions are published with the model), from which clusters whose structures were all more than half coil had been removed. Fine-tuning used molecular dynamics: 1,093 CATH domains of up to 199 residues, 271 MEGAscale wild types with 21,458 point mutants, 1,100 octapeptides, and published simulations of a few named proteins (DDR1 kinases, SETD8, coronavirus proteins, MHC class II, barnase–barstar). A last stage fitted measured folding stabilities of 361 MEGAscale wild-type domains and their mutants [11]. The DESRES fast-folder simulations trained a separate model only. I read the sequences of each part (the simulated topologies, the cluster members from UniProt) and described them as I described the SAXS set: CATH superfamilies, chain length, disorder predicted from sequence by one predictor for every set [12], and organism.

  • Disorder is nearly absent from the training data. 1.7% of the AFDB input chains are predicted mostly disordered and 6.7% carry a disordered run of at least 30 residues; of the simulated CATH domains, 0.3% and 0.5%. The SAXS constructs: 15.5% and 19.1%.
  • Simulated chains are short. The simulated CATH domains have a median of 100 residues and none reaches 200; the MEGAscale domains reach 74. The AFDB inputs are full-length chains (median 261), 20% of them longer than 500 residues, each seen as predicted structures without dynamics. No SAXS construct exceeds 500 residues.
  • Pre-training is bacterial. 81% of the AFDB clusters come from bacteria other than E. coli and 0.2% from human proteins; human domains make up 15% of the simulated set and 40% of the SAXS profiles.
  • Mainly-β domains are thin, α/β enzyme folds are not. Mainly-β domains are 11% of the AFDB units and 17% of the simulated ones, against 23% of CATH and 33% of the SAXS set. The Rossmann fold is 16% of AFDB units and 14% of simulated ones, above CATH (13%); the TIM barrel is 1.6% of AFDB units and absent from the simulations (2.9% of CATH).
  • Most of the archive's superfamilies occur in training, few in the simulations. Of the 215 CATH superfamilies in the SAXS constructs, 146 occur in the AFDB clusters, 67 in the simulated domains and 157 in some part of the training data; 58 occur in none.

Where the SAXS archive sits against the training data and CATH

As the reference for experimentally known structure space I use CATH 4.4.0 at the S35 level (domains clustered at 35% sequence identity) for folds, and non-redundant PDB clusters (30% identity) and Swiss-Prot for organism, length and disorder. CATH and the PDB describe what has been solved; the comparison with the training data is above.

  • Common folds are covered, rare ones are not. 72% of the 399 profiles carry a CATH superfamily inside the construct. The 215 superfamilies present are 3.2% of CATH's 6,630 but hold 33% of its S35 clusters: 34 of the 50 most populated superfamilies are present (68%), 85 of the top 200, and 43 of the 4,630 ranked beyond 2,000 (0.9%).
  • Mainly-β domains are enriched and α/β enzyme folds depleted. Mainly-β domains make up 33% of the set against 23% of CATH (ratio 1.48, 95% interval 1.26–1.71), α/β domains 40% against 52% (0.77, 0.67–0.87). The Rossmann fold appears 26 times where 44 are expected, the TIM barrel 3 times against 10, and the NAD(P)-binding Rossmann superfamily not at all. The most over-represented superfamilies include SH3, EF-hand, protein kinase and PH domains; 20 of the 26 profiles that carry one are of human proteins.
  • Human proteins dominate. 40% of the profiles are of human proteins (35%–45%), against 16% of PDB clusters and 3.5% of Swiss-Prot.
  • The constructs are fragments of long multidomain proteins. No construct is longer than 500 residues (12% of PDB clusters and 20% of Swiss-Prot proteins are); the median construct has 252 residues, the full-length protein it comes from 448. The full-length proteins carry 4.1 CATH domains on average, 27% of them four or more, against 1.6 and 8% for Swiss-Prot; the constructs carry 1.4.
  • Disorder is over-represented. By UniProt annotation 6.4% of the constructs are mostly disordered (4.4–9.3%), against 1.6% of Swiss-Prot; 45% of the full-length proteins carry a long disordered region or are mostly disordered, against 14% of Swiss-Prot, and the constructs keep part of it (20%).
  • A quarter of the measured constructs have no experimental structure. For 100 of 390 mapped profiles (26%, 22%–30%) no PDB structure covers half of the construct, and for 75 none overlaps it. The share rises with disorder: folded 41 of 241 (17%); partly disordered 34 of 108 (31%); disordered 25 of 41 (61%).

Interpretation. Set against the measured composition of the training data, three of the archive's skews fall where the training data are thinnest: disorder (1.7% of AFDB input chains and 0.3% of simulated domains predicted mostly disordered, against 15.5% of the constructs), human proteins (0.2% of AFDB clusters, 15% of simulated domains, 40% of the profiles) and mainly-β domains (11% of AFDB units, 17% of simulated ones, 33% of the set). The depletion of α/β enzyme folds is a gap of the archive only: the Rossmann fold is 16% of AFDB units and 14% of simulated ones, above its CATH share. Long chains are present in pre-training as single predicted structures (20% of AFDB inputs above 500 residues) and absent from both the simulations and the archive.

Mapping, definitions and database versions

390 of 399 profiles map to a UniProtKB entry: 353 through the accession in the SASBDB record, 23 through a PDB sequence search (identity ≥ 90%) and the SIFTS reference of the hit, and 14 through a UniProt peptide search; a local alignment to the canonical sequence then defines the construct region (median identity 1.00). For 17 profiles the SASBDB accession was set aside because it pointed to a UniProtKB entry deleted since deposition or aligned to a small part of the construct; all but 1 of them were mapped again by sequence search. The 9 unmapped profiles are SASDAT3 (immunoglobulin- like filamin two-domain …), SASDCV7 (TET12(2.3)SN-f5b), SASDDL7 (anti-DISC1 single-domain camelid antibody VHH …), SASDKX6 (PSK, an antimicrobial peptide from Chrysomya …), SASDM97 (Recombinant monoclonal anti-proNGF antibody …), SASDMT7 (Lanthionine synthetase C-like protein), SASDNW2 (Fab fragment in complex with small molecule …), SASDS37 (Harpin Z2), SASDSV6 (Anti-Idiotypic-Palivizumab-Nanobody1). Domains are CATH-Gene3D assignments whose residues lie at least half inside the construct region; PDB coverage counts residues of atomic-model chains listed by SIFTS.

How close are these proteins to BioEmu-1's training data?

For each construct I searched every part of the training data for the most similar sequence over a local alignment that covers at least half of the construct [13], and checked whether the construct's CATH superfamilies occur there. BioEmu-1's training data were filtered against the paper's own test proteins only, so overlap with these proteins was possible.

  • Most measured proteins are far from the training data. Of the 399 profiles, 165 (41%) have a training sequence of at least 30% identity, 66 (17%) of at least 50%, 23 (6%) of at least 90% and 11 an identical stretch covering at least half the construct. The close neighbours are AFDB cluster members and named proteins of the published simulations (5 of the 23 at 90% or more, all coronavirus proteins); only 23 constructs reach 30% to a simulated CATH domain or MegaSim wild type, and 2 of 390 UniProt accessions are AFDB cluster members.
  • Disordered proteins are the furthest. 32 of the 41 disordered constructs have no training sequence at 30% identity.
  • Superfamilies: the construct carries a CATH superfamily that occurs in the training data for 254 profiles, one that does not for 35, and none for 110; restricted to the simulated superfamilies, 143 and 146.

Pooled, the raw fit improves with closeness: χ² ≤ 2 is met by 32% of profiles below 30% identity and 52% at 90% or more (Spearman ρ +0.11, p 0.02), and the Rg ratio falls slightly (ρ -0.12, p 0.01); raw χ² itself does not reach significance (p 0.08). The bins differ in disorder class: 32 of the 234 profiles below 30% are disordered and 2 of the 23 at 90% or more. Within classes no measure varies with closeness: across the 12 within-class Spearman tests (three classes, raw χ², raw fit, NRMSD and Rg ratio) the smallest nominal p is 0.03 (disordered, NRMSD) and every Holm-adjusted p is at least 0.35; a rank test stratified by class finds no difference in raw χ² between constructs with a training neighbour of at least 50% identity and the rest (van Elteren p 0.17). Superfamily presence does not separate the errors either (pooled Mann–Whitney p 0.97; restricted to simulated superfamilies p 0.13, stratified by class p 0.12).

In this archive, closeness to the training data does not explain BioEmu-1's raw error beyond the disorder class. The over-extended disordered ensembles are also the proteins furthest from the training data, and the archive cannot separate the two: only 9 disordered constructs have a training neighbour at 30% identity or more.

Does a solved structure matter?

Of the 390 mapped profiles, 290 have an experimental structure covering at least half of the construct, 25 a partial one and 75 none. Pooled, BioEmu-1's raw ensemble meets χ² ≤ 2 for 41% (35%–46%) of the first group, 20% (9%–39%) of the second and 28% (19%–39%) of the third, with median raw χ² 2.8, 8.9 and 4.1 (at least half covered against the rest, two-sided Mann–Whitney p 0.01). The groups differ in disorder: a structure covers at least half of the construct for 83% of folded, 69% of partly disordered and 39% of disordered profiles. Within classes the difference vanishes for folded (p 0.35) and partly disordered proteins (p 0.31; here the median χ² is higher with a structure, 5.3 against 3.0), and a rank test stratified by class finds no difference in raw χ² (van Elteren p 0.39) or in the Rg ratio (p 0.38). NRMSD does not differ even pooled (p 0.54).

Among disordered proteins, raw χ² is lower when a structure exists (median 5.0 against 12.4, p 0.04, n = 16 against 25), but the difference does not survive a Holm correction over the six within-class tests (p 0.22) and is absent under NRMSD (p 0.86). At the median these ensembles remain larger than measured: Rg ratio 1.15 with a structure (95% interval 0.97–1.25, which reaches 1) and 1.22 (1.12–1.39) without; the two do not differ (p 0.18). Whether the construct has an experimental structure does not explain BioEmu-1's raw error beyond what the disorder class explains.

Which protein data to collect

Each row joins three measurements: how much of the category the training data contain, how much the archive measures, and BioEmu-1's raw error on it here. A category is kept when the training data are thin in it and either the error on it exceeds the error on the rest of the archive or the archive holds no measurement of it. The order is my judgement from that evidence: the first row combines the thinnest training data with the largest error and a direction SAXS reads directly; the third is a gap in both the simulations and the archive, so its error is unknown. I give no numeric priority: the heuristic priority score tested above picked high-discrepancy profiles no better than random choice.

Four candidates from the coverage analysis are not supported: α/β enzyme folds (Rossmann, TIM barrel), bacteria other than E. coli, superfamilies beyond the 200 most populated, proteins with no experimental structure. Either the training data are not thin in them (the Rossmann fold is more frequent in pre-training and simulation than in CATH; 81% of the pre-training clusters are bacterial) or BioEmu-1's raw error on them matches or is below the error on the rest of the archive. Human proteins and mainly-β domains are thin in pre-training, but the error on them matches the rest; so does the error on constructs with two or more domains up to 500 residues.

Feasibility · disordered and full-length proteins

  • Disordered proteins are hard to produce and to measure well: they are degraded by proteases, some aggregate, and they scatter weakly, so the data need size-exclusion-coupled SAXS and a concentration series. Crystallography cannot resolve them.
  • The archive shows such data can be obtained but drop out more often: 41 of 49 disordered entries (84%, 95% interval 71%–91%) pass the quality checks, against 249 of 268 folded entries (93%, 89%–95%; two-sided Fisher exact p 0.048). All 8 disordered entries that fail do so on the mass check: the molecular mass recorded with the profile exceeds 1.6 times the sequence mass.
  • NMR and single-molecule FRET are the main experimental alternatives.
  • Simulation is a complementary source: all-atom force fields tuned for disorder, such as a99SB-disp [14] and CHARMM36m [15], or the coarse-grained CALVADOS model [16], validated against SAXS and NMR data that already exist.
  • For full-length multidomain proteins the counterpart is rigid-body modelling of known domain structures against a SAXS profile, for example with CORAL [17].

How such data would be used. BioEmu-1's last training stage fitted measured folding stabilities by property-prediction fine-tuning: a foldedness observable computed from sampled structures is matched to the measurement by back-propagating through the sampler [1]. A SAXS observable could enter the same way, as the radius of gyration of the sampled conformers or, through a differentiable forward model, as the scattering curve. Reweighting the ensemble toward a measured profile, as in the reweighting section, gives a second route: the reweighted conformers serve as conformer-level targets. Neither route was tried in this study; the rows above are where either would add information the training data lack.

The campaign

The error map identifies where BioEmu-1 disagrees with deposited data; it cannot yet say where it will disagree on a new protein. The campaign has two arms that follow from that. Arm 2 tests the size bias in the category this analysis ranks first, disordered proteins; Arm 1 checks that deposited profiles reproduce under controlled conditions, which any profile needs before it can serve as a training label. The full proposal gives constructs, assay, scripted quality criteria, success criteria, contingencies and work packages for an external provider.

Arm 1 · replication: are known discrepancies reproducible under controlled conditions?

High-error, reweightable monomers from the archive are re-measured by SEC-SAXS in one standard buffer and temperature, with tags removed and a concentration series. Standardised measurement reduces condition heterogeneity and tests whether the discrepancy is reproducible. One common buffer and temperature can itself shift some ensembles, so each new profile is compared with the deposited one before it is compared with the model. The first 12 are in the campaign proposal.

Arm 2 · hypothesis test: are BioEmu-1's disordered ensembles systematically too extended?

The hypothesis came from this archive, so the arm is a prospective replication test with pre-specified model-based selection and new SAXS measurements. Test proteins are disordered proteins whose BioEmu-1 ensemble Rg exceeds the scaling-law Rg for disordered chains (1.927 N0.598 Å [9]) by more than 10%, a quantity computed from the model and the sequence alone, drawn from the archive's disordered entries whose deposited profiles pass the quality checks, spanning chain length and net charge (19 of 41 disordered entries qualify). The scaling-law-matched controls are disordered proteins of the same length bins whose ensemble Rg is within 10% of the scaling law (13 qualify). In the archive their ratio of ensemble Rg to measured Rg is 1.19 at the median, against 1.36 for the test group, so the controls are not known to agree with experiment. Pre-specified outcome: the median Rgexp/Rgmodel across the test arm from Guinier fits of the new profiles. The bias is refuted if that median is at least 0.95; it is confirmed if it is at most 0.90 in the test arm and at least 0.95 in the controls.

Feasibility judgement

  • A single common buffer and temperature is the aim, but it may not hold for every protein: some may be insoluble, unstable or aggregate in it.
  • Gate before any SAXS: solubility in the standard buffer; the A280 trace of purification and analytical SEC (one symmetric peak at the expected elution volume) with the A260/A280 ratio for nucleic acid; SDS-PAGE (one band at the expected mass); circular dichroism where the fold is in question.
  • Aggregation signs on the SAXS data: a low-angle upturn, a non-linear Guinier region, Rg or I(0)/c rising with concentration, a mass from I(0) above the monomer, or Rg changing across the SEC peak; all are among the scripted quality criteria.
  • Fallback: a protein that fails in the standard buffer is measured in the nearest buffer in which it is monodisperse, or in its deposited buffer, with the deviation recorded, and analysed separately; one that fails in every buffer is replaced by the next eligible system.

Both arms use size-exclusion-coupled SAXS at three concentrations with a protein standard in every session, and eight scripted quality criteria (Guinier linearity, no low-angle upturn and Rg agreeing across concentrations, no radiation damage across frames, molecular weight from I(0) within 20% of the sequence mass, no negative intensities, a repeated deposited entry reproduced at χ² < 2, I(0)/c constant across concentrations, and a constant Rg across the SEC peak). Entries whose target fit is not reached get hydrogen–deuterium exchange mass spectrometry on the same batch of protein. Every batch of twelve constructs re-runs this pipeline, so the error map is updated before the next batch is chosen.

How does BioEmu-1 compare with other ensemble generators?

The archive carries computed curves from other models for the same entries, scored here identically and without reweighting: the ensemble generators Boltz-2, IDPFold, idpSAM, PepTron, and the single-structure predictors AlphaFold2 and ESMFold as reference baselines. On the shared entries BioEmu-1 has the lowest median raw χ² of the seven, and the ordering is kept under NRMSD. PepTron comes closest: it beats BioEmu-1 on 40% of the 399 shared entries (95% interval 36%–45%). BioEmu-1 is the only tested model with a disordered median Rg ratio above 1.1; PepTron sits at 1.01.

AF-CALVADOS [10] was evaluated on this benchmark but its predictions were not in the archive.

Limits

The ensembles are those in the PeptoneBench archive, which records the BioEmu code version but not the checkpoint; re-sampling with the current v1.2 checkpoint is the first follow-up. SASBDB profiles differ in buffer, temperature and construct, none of which the model sees, so part of the raw error is condition mismatch. The forward model is treated as exact; its hydration-shell parameters bias Rg by a few per cent, which is why modestly reweightable cases are read with care. Disorder classes come from a sequence-based predictor. The model comparison is restricted to the six comparators on the shared entries. CATH and the PDB serve as the reference for experimentally known structure space. BioEmu-1's training data were measured from their public releases: the AFDB cluster definitions and the simulated systems are those published with the model, the 361 MEGAscale wild types used for fine-tuning are a subset of the curated set the paper does not list, and the other published simulations are represented by the full UniProt chains of the named proteins, an upper bound on their overlap. Disorder of the training chains is predicted from sequence, without examining the training structures, and AFDB superfamilies are the CATH-Gene3D assignments of the full chain. PDB coverage of a construct comes from SIFTS residue ranges, which count residues listed in the structure record and can include residues not modelled in the coordinates. The prediction and selection tests are retrospective and use 399 entries; a predictor that fails at this size could succeed with more data or with richer features of the model's own ensemble. Profiles with a low-angle upturn above 10%, an intensity more than three standard errors below zero, a reported error of zero or less, no valid Guinier region, or a measured mass above 1.6 times the sequence mass are kept out of every statistic (1, 12, 1, 7 and 18 profiles; 37 in all, as some carry more than one flag).

Reproducibility

The pipeline runs in named stages (download, score, coordinate radii, analysis, selection test, prediction, envelopes, report) from a locked environment, with unit tests on synthetic data. Derived results are tracked in the repository, and the page build reads every number from them and stops if a sentence that states a direction or a comparison no longer matches. Key code: coordinate radii, acquisition policies, error prediction. The ensembles and computed curves are those published by the PeptoneBench authors [3] (Zenodo 17306061, CC-BY 4.0).
